# Assessing Legal Meaning Preservation in English and Hindi Simplifications of Indian Statutes

## Abstract

Plain-language versions of statutes can widen access to the law, but a simplification that drops a condition, turns an obligation into a permission or alters a time limit misleads the reader while still looking fluent. JUDGEBERT (Beauchemin et al., 2025) introduced a learned metric for legal meaning preservation (LMP) on French insurance text. We extend that line of work to Indian statutory law in two languages. From the official texts of the Right to Information Act, 2005 and the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 we build a corpus of original-simplification pairs in three deliberately contrasting styles: a standard zero-shot simplification, an aggressive "explain to a twelve-year-old" simplification, and a simplification carrying exactly one rule-injected legal error of a known type. Each pair is scored on JUDGEBERT's 1-10 rubric; for this version of the work the scores are produced by two disclosed large-language-model annotators rather than by humans, which is a deviation from our original human-judgement protocol and is reported as such throughout. We train multilingual cross-encoders on clause-grouped splits and compare them against generic similarity metrics and an LLM judge given the same rubric. [TBD: headline result.] We additionally report zero-shot transfer between English and Hindi, transfer across the two acts, sanity checks on identical and unrelated pairs, and a qualitative analysis of at least fifteen legally difficult cases. We also document two reproducibility traps that silently destroy such experiments: a character-level tokenizer fallback that collapses cross-encoder training, and legacy-font Hindi PDF text layers that lose characters without raising any error.

**Keywords—** legal NLP, text simplification, meaning preservation, evaluation metrics, Hindi, multilingual transformers, cross-encoder regression

## I. Introduction

Indian statutes are drafted in long, heavily qualified sentences, and the official Hindi versions are no easier to read than the English. Large language models can rewrite such text into plain language, and doing so at scale is attractive for access to justice. The risk is that the rewriting is judged by the wrong yardstick. Generic similarity metrics reward lexical and semantic overlap, so a simplification that preserves almost every word but deletes a proviso scores well, even though the legal consequence has changed.

JUDGEBERT made this concrete. On FrJUDGE, a corpus of 297 French insurance sentence blocks scored by five law students, BERTScore correlates with human LMP judgements at Pearson 0.46 and SBERT at 0.13, while a CamemBERT-v2 cross-encoder trained directly on the rubric reaches 0.74. BERTScore and MeaningBERT over-score the human label on 82% of test pairs; the learned metric does so on none. The lesson is that legal meaning preservation is a distinct target that has to be learned, not approximated by similarity.

We ask whether that result carries to a different legal system, a different pair of languages and a different kind of statutory text, and we attack the specific weaknesses of the original study. Each gap below maps to a contribution of this paper.

- JUDGEBERT covers French and a single domain. We cover English and Hindi across two Indian central acts. Because the Hindi statute is an official translation of the same provision, the language comparison is controlled rather than confounded by content.
- FrJUDGE contains one simplification style, so its label distribution is narrow. We add aggressive simplifications, which tend to drop conditions, and perturbed simplifications carrying exactly one injected legal error of a known type. The latter is a labelled diagnostic set: it tells us which legal error types a metric is blind to.
- Krippendorff's alpha on FrJUDGE LMP was 0.10, with annotators splitting into a lenient and a strict group. We therefore treat agreement as a first-class result rather than a footnote, and we report it for whichever annotator population we actually used.
- FrJUDGE splits are pair-level, so a test original can reappear in training as an identical augmentation pair, and the headline 0.97 Pearson of the augmented model is measured on a test set that contains trivial identical and unrelated pairs. Our splits are grouped by source clause and verified disjoint at clause and text level, and sanity checks are reported separately on holdout provisions used nowhere else.
- JUDGEBERT reports no out-of-domain test. We train on one act and test on the other.

Our contributions are therefore: (i) a bilingual legal LMP corpus with a documented, blinded scoring protocol and an explicit statement of who, or what, produced the labels; (ii) a JUDGEBERT-style multilingual cross-encoder for LMP; (iii) a comparison against generic metrics and an LLM judge given the identical rubric; (iv) cross-lingual, cross-domain and sanity experiments; and (v) a qualitative error analysis. We also report, in Section VII, two failures of our own pipeline that would have produced confidently wrong numbers, because both are invisible unless specifically tested for.

## II. Related Work

### A. Evaluating simplification

Simplification quality is usually decomposed into simplicity, fluency and meaning preservation. Meaning preservation is commonly measured by n-gram overlap, by contextual embedding similarity such as BERTScore, by sentence-embedding cosine similarity, or by learned or question-based metrics such as QuestEval, LENS and MeaningBERT. BLESS benchmarks large language models as sentence simplifiers with zero-shot prompts; we reuse its prompt so that our normal variant is comparable to established practice.

### B. Legal meaning preservation

JUDGEBERT is the direct predecessor of this work. Its rubric, which we adopt unchanged, first places a simplification in a bracket (Accurate 7-10, Imprecise 2-6, Off-track 1) and then subtracts one point per identified error, with a floor of 1; the error types are omission, hallucination, consistency issue and confusion. Its model is a cross-encoder regression over the concatenated sentence pair. Its augmentation adds identical pairs labelled 10 and unrelated pairs labelled 0, the latter mined from Quebec legal texts with ROUGE below 0.25 and BLEU below 25.

### C. Indian legal NLP

Work on Indian legal text has concentrated on judgments: domain-adapted encoders such as InLegalBERT, and benchmarks such as IL-TUR, target tasks like judgment prediction, rhetorical-role labelling and summarisation. Statutory simplification, and the question of whether a simplification is legally faithful, is comparatively unexplored for Indian law, and we are not aware of a Hindi resource for it.

### D. Multilingual encoders

For the backbone we consider XLM-R, which is multilingual but not Indic-focused, and MuRIL and IndicBERT v2, which are trained with Indian languages and transliteration in mind. LaBSE provides a strong language-agnostic sentence embedding and serves as one of our baselines.

## III. Dataset

### A. Sources and provenance

We use two central acts from different legal domains, each chosen because an official Hindi version exists: the Right to Information Act, 2005 (public information) and the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (consumer law). India Code is the canonical repository for both, but it was unreachable while this version of the corpus was built, so we used other official government sources and recorded exactly which. Table I lists them.

**TABLE I. Sources, editions and extraction yield**

| Document | Edition | Sections | Units |
|---|---|---|---|
| RTI Act 2005, English (DoPT) | As on 18 Nov 2025; includes the 2023 amendment | 31 | 109 |
| RTI Act 2005, Hindi (DoPT) | Carries the 2019 amendments; sec. 8(1) is the older wording; text layer unusable, read by OCR (Tesseract 5.4, tessdata_best hin) | 27 | 101 |
| Consumer Protection Act 2019, English (Gazette) | Act 35 of 2019, 9 Aug 2019; original enactment | 107 | 229 |
| Consumer Protection Act 2019, Hindi | Not obtainable; India Code unreachable | -- | -- |

Two consequences follow and are carried through the rest of the paper. First, the official Hindi text of the Consumer Protection Act could not be obtained, so that act contributes English-only material and the English-Hindi comparison (E2) is confined to the Right to Information Act. Second, the two Right to Information copies are not the same edition: the English consolidation is current to 18 November 2025 and includes the 2023 amendment, whereas the Hindi copy, although it carries the 2019 amendments in its footnotes, retains the older personal-information wording in section 8(1). Provisions affected by this are flagged automatically and dropped at review rather than silently reconciled, because editing one language to match the other would fabricate statutory text.

### B. Extraction

Each PDF is converted to sub-section units, the unit of analysis being a numbered sub-section such as section 7(1), with its marginal or inline heading attached. English and Hindi units of the same provision share a key, which is what makes the bilingual alignment automatic. Three details were needed for real government PDFs and are worth recording, since each cost us a parser bug. Cross-references of the form "sub-section (3) of section 8" must not be read as the start of a new sub-section. Amendment markers, footnote blocks and the arrangement-of-sections table at the front of an act must be stripped, but the word "Repeal" must not be mistaken for the footnote abbreviation "Rep.". The Gazette printing of the Consumer Protection Act places section headings in the page margin rather than inline, so for that document we extract with a geometry-aware backend that reads the marginal headings and the marginal statute citations separately from the body column, and fails loudly if a numbered section is found without a heading.

### C. The Hindi text layer

The Hindi PDF is not scanned, yet its text layer cannot be used as it stands, and the way it fails is instructive. Extracted with Poppler's pdftotext, 4.9% of all Devanagari characters emerge as U+FFFD replacement characters: 2461 characters across 100 of 102 units, an irreversible loss. Extracted with PyMuPDF, nothing is lost, but the legacy Mangal glyphs are mapped into the Vedic and Sundanese Unicode blocks (2681 characters drawn from only 48 distinct code points) and the vowel signs appear in visual rather than logical order. In other words the page is readable to a human and systematically wrong to a machine. Our extractor therefore computes a Devanagari ratio and a misplaced-vowel-sign ratio for every Hindi document and refuses the text layer when it fails either test; both routes above are correctly rejected. We report this because a pipeline that silently accepted either extraction would have produced a Hindi corpus of fluent-looking nonsense, and no downstream metric would have revealed it.

The Hindi text used in this work therefore comes from optical character recognition: the pages are rendered at 300 dpi and read with Tesseract 5.4 using the high-quality tessdata_best Hindi model, which the predecessor literature and our own trials both prefer over the fast model for legal vocabulary. This clears the acceptance test decisively: Devanagari ratio 0.993, misplaced-vowel-sign ratio 0.000 and no replacement characters at all. One systematic OCR defect remains and is worth naming, because it attacks precisely the part of a statute that must not be approximated: the digit 1 is frequently dropped or misread, so section 12 is read as 2, section 13 as 03 and the sub-section marker (1) as an empty pair of brackets. We therefore repair numbering from the sequence rather than from appearance, restoring a number only when the observed token is a recognised one-digit-drop variant of the number the sequence expects, and we do not touch anything else. Every repair is logged.

### D. Clause selection

A provision is eligible if it has one to five sentences, 15 to 90 English words and a Flesch reading-ease score of at most 50, so that the simplification task is non-trivial; if it is not boilerplate (short title, extent, definitions, rule-making powers, repeal and savings); and if its text is not duplicated elsewhere in either act. The duplicate test matters more than it sounds: statutes reuse standard provisos verbatim, and two identical provisions in different splits would leak the test set into training even though the split is grouped by clause. At most three clauses are taken per section, and sampling is weighted towards provisions containing exceptions, overrides, conditions and time limits, which is where legal meaning is most fragile. We oversample by a factor of 1.3 to absorb losses at review.

Every candidate then passes a review step that is the only place where a clause can be accepted. The selection tool pre-computes warning flags (replacement characters, Latin characters inside Hindi text, numbers that differ between the two languages, missing Hindi counterpart, known edition mismatch) and never sets the keep decision itself. In the design this review is performed by a human. Under the project deadline it was performed instead by a rule-based agent script, and we disclose that: rows that are misaligned, fragmentary, contain Latin characters inside Hindi or fall in the section where the two editions differ are dropped, with the reason recorded per row. The only text repairs permitted are the numbering repairs described above, and only where the Hindi number differs from its English counterpart by an OCR-dropped 1; seven such repairs were made and each is logged with the before and after text. A sample of kept rows was then checked against the source pages. No agent at any point edited statutory wording.

The resulting corpus is 78 clauses: 38 from the Right to Information Act, of which 35 have an aligned Hindi counterpart, and 40 from the Consumer Protection Act, which are English-only because its Hindi text was unobtainable. That gives 113 clause-language items and, with three variants each, 339 pairs, above the 300 the study design calls for. Table II breaks this down.

### E. Simplifications

For each selected clause and each available language we generate three variants. The normal variant uses the zero-shot BLESS prompt, translated for Hindi. The aggressive variant asks for an explanation to a twelve-year-old in at most two sentences, which reliably sacrifices conditions and therefore populates the low end of the scale that FrJUDGE lacks. The perturbed variant takes a normal simplification and injects exactly one legal error, balanced across five types: modality (shall or must becomes may, and the reverse), negation, a changed number, deletion of an exception, proviso or override, and narrowed scope. The Hindi rules operate only on clause-final verb groups, so that, for example, karega becomes kar sakega without touching unrelated words that merely contain the same letters. The idiom "as may be prescribed" is explicitly exempted, because the may in it confers no permission.

Our output caps are 200 tokens for English and 500 for Hindi, rather than JUDGEBERT's 100, because our clauses reach 90 words and Devanagari consumes more tokens per word; truncated generations are recorded and reported rather than silently kept. One further deviation must be stated: JUDGEBERT sampled its simplifications from gpt-4-turbo through an API at temperature 1.0 and top-p 0.9, whereas ours were written by a Claude Opus 5.5 agent following the same prompts, with no sampling parameters to record. The prompt identifier, the model string and a timestamp are stored with every generation, and the temperature and top-p fields are null rather than invented. Our simplifications are consequently likely to be more conservative than temperature-1.0 samples, which plausibly shifts the label distribution upward relative to FrJUDGE. [TBD: number truncated.]

### F. Scoring protocol and its deviation from human judgement

This is the point at which the present version of the work departs from our protocol, and we state it plainly rather than in a footnote. The intended design was three human annotators per pair after a shared calibration round. Because of the project deadline, the LMP scores used here were produced by two disclosed large-language-model annotators, Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra, each filling its own blinded workbook under the same rubric and conventions written for the human annotators. This does not satisfy the requirement of agreement with human legal judgement, and no claim in this paper should be read as establishing it.

The blinding is real and mechanical rather than a matter of trust. Each annotator receives only an opaque pair identifier, in an order shuffled per annotator with items from the same clause separated; the variant name, the injected error type and the answer key are in files the annotators never read, and neither annotator sees the other's workbook. The score is not entered directly: the annotator chooses a bracket and counts errors by type, and the score is recomputed from those entries by our own code, so a rubric change cannot be lost in a spreadsheet formula. Two further constraints follow from using models as annotators. Model families overlap between generation and annotation, so any annotator that also generated the text it scores cannot be called blind, and we disclose that overlap rather than assuming it away. And an LLM judge may not be evaluated against labels from its own model, since that measures self-consistency and not meaning preservation; our judge baseline therefore uses a different model from either annotator.

Agreement between the two model annotators is reported as LLM-annotator agreement and never as human agreement. With only two annotators a leave-one-out human ceiling cannot be computed, so the ceiling we would compare models against is simply unavailable in this version. To keep a path to the original claim open, a separate 30-pair validation workbook is prepared for human legal annotators; if it is scored we report the correlation between the model labels and the human scores on it, and if it is not we report its absence as a limitation. ### G. Augmentation, sanity holdouts and splits

Following JUDGEBERT we add, for each clause and language, an identical pair labelled 10 and an unrelated pair whose partner is a provision with ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2 and ROUGE-L below 0.25 and BLEU below 25. We label unrelated pairs 1 rather than 0, because 1 is the floor of the rubric and an unreachable 0 would distort the regression; a flag reproduces the original choice. These overlap statistics are computed with a Devanagari-aware tokenizer: the widely used rouge_score package discards non-ASCII text, which would classify every Hindi pair as unrelated and quietly poison the augmentation set.

The sanity holdouts are built only from provisions that are not selected, are not in a section containing a selected clause, and are not used as augmentation partners, so that passing a sanity check cannot be an artefact of memorising training text. Splits are 60/10/30 by clause over five seeds, and every pair derived from one clause, both languages, all three variants and its augmentation pairs, stays within a single split; the splitter asserts this at clause level and at text level. Headline metrics are computed on annotated test pairs only, with augmentation and sanity pairs excluded and reported separately.

## IV. Method

### A. LMP model

The model follows JUDGEBERT: the pair is encoded as original, separator, simplification by a pretrained multilingual encoder, and a linear regression head on the pooled representation predicts the score under mean-squared-error loss, with predictions clipped to the rubric range 1 to 10. We keep the published optimisation settings, namely AdamW at learning rate 5e-5, batch size 16, linear decay without warm-up, gradient clipping at norm 1.0, and up to 100 epochs retaining the checkpoint with the best development loss. Candidate backbones are XLM-R, MuRIL and IndicBERT v2; each is trained with and without augmentation over five clause-grouped seeds. Model selection uses the annotated development set by default, with a flag to select on the augmented development set as the original work did, because the two choices are not equivalent and the difference should be visible.

### B. Baselines

We compare against four reference points of increasing sophistication. ROUGE-L and BLEU, computed with our Devanagari-aware tokenizer, represent pure overlap. LaBSE cosine similarity represents language-agnostic sentence semantics. Multilingual BERTScore F1 represents contextual token matching and is the strongest generic metric in the original study. Finally an LLM judge receives the annotators' rubric verbatim, at temperature 0, and returns a bracket and error counts from which the score is recomputed by the same function used for the annotators; this is the most interesting comparison, because it asks whether a general model with the rubric in its prompt can replace a model trained on the rubric. Every baseline is mapped onto the 1-10 scale twice, once naively and once by a linear calibration fitted on the training split only, and both are reported, since an uncalibrated metric can correlate well while having a meaningless RMSE.

### C. Decisions and reporting

For the decision output we map the continuous prediction onto the rubric brackets: at least 7 is Preserved, 2 up to 7 is Partially Preserved, below 2 is Not Preserved. Alongside Pearson and RMSE we report Spearman and MAE, and the over-scoring rate, that is the share of pairs whose prediction exceeds the label, because the practically dangerous failure for this task is a metric that flatters a simplification which has lost a condition. All aggregate numbers are means with standard deviations over the five seeds, and results are broken down by language, by act and by variant.

## V. Experiments

Five experiments are defined in advance. E1 compares the generic baselines and the LLM judge against the trained cross-encoder on the random clause-grouped splits. E2 reports per-language results and zero-shot transfer in both directions, training on English and testing on Hindi and the reverse, which is possible precisely because the two languages contain the same provisions; it is confined to the Right to Information Act for the reason given in Section III-A. E3 trains on one act and tests on the other in both directions. E4 runs the sanity checks on the disjoint holdouts, reporting the share of identical pairs scored at least 9.9 and of unrelated pairs scored at most 1.1. E5 is a qualitative analysis of at least fifteen legally difficult cases, grouped by injected error type and by the most important change each annotator recorded, which the perturbed variant makes systematic rather than anecdotal.

## VII. Reproducibility Notes

Two defects in our own pipeline produced plausible-looking but worthless results, and both are worth reporting because neither announces itself.

The first is a tokenizer fallback. Under transformers 5.x, loading the CamemBERT-v2 checkpoint through the generic auto-tokenizer yields a byte-level tokenizer without its merge table, which splits text into single characters. A sentence pair then exceeds 650 tokens, is truncated at the maximum length, and training collapses onto predicting the label mean: the training error equals the label variance and the test correlation is slightly negative. Nothing errors out. Our loader now detects this case and falls back to the checkpoint's own tokenizer file, and we verify the token count for any new backbone.

The second is the Hindi text layer described in Section III-C, where two different extractors fail in two different ways while both returning text that looks like Hindi. The general lesson for legal NLP in Indic scripts is that an extraction step needs an explicit, quantitative acceptance test, because downstream metrics are computed happily on corrupted input.

As an end-to-end check of the training code against a published result, we convert the released FrJUDGE splits and reproduce the original setting without augmentation. [TBD: our Pearson and RMSE against the published 0.74 +/- 0.02 and 1.72.] The FrJUDGE data is CC-BY-NC-SA 4.0 and is used only for this check; we do not redistribute it.

## VIII. Limitations and Ethics

- The LMP labels in this version are disclosed model judgements, not human legal judgements. The central claim of the predecessor work, agreement with human legal judgement, is therefore not tested here, and the planned 30-pair human validation set is the minimum needed to begin testing it.
- Two model annotators give no leave-one-out ceiling, and their agreement may reflect shared pretraining rather than a well-defined construct. Model-family overlap between the generator and an annotator is disclosed where it occurs.
- The corpus covers two acts and, for Hindi, one act only, because the official Hindi text of the Consumer Protection Act was unavailable. The two Right to Information editions differ, and the Hindi text had to be recovered by OCR; both are documented and flagged, and affected provisions are dropped rather than edited.
- The clause review that gates the corpus was performed by a rule-based agent rather than a human, and the simplifications were written by an agent rather than sampled from an API at a recorded temperature. Both are disclosed above. A human pass over the kept clauses and over a sample of simplifications is the first thing we would add.
- The Hindi text is OCR output. Although it passes our acceptance tests and its numbering was repaired from the sequence, OCR error in legal vocabulary cannot be excluded, and a Hindi legal reader has not yet verified the kept clauses.
- Injected errors are rule-based and may be easier to detect than errors a model makes naturally, so perturbed results are reported separately from the rest.
- Statute texts are public government documents. The corpus is a course research artefact for evaluating simplification quality; it is not a validated legal tool, and a predicted LMP score is not legal advice.
